Slide 1 · Arrival task

Using your eWorkbook

Private Game Board stays private

Pre-session, 5 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Orient participants to the eWorkbook before the formal start so technology issues do not slow the first activity.

Run it

  • Greet participants as they enter and ask them to open the eWorkbook link from chat.
  • Point out the three items on the screen: section navigation, workspace fields, and Download my work.
  • Tell participants to save and download their work before breaks and at the end of the day.
  • Do not teach the full workspace yet. The formal walkthrough happens later.
  • Use this as an arrival task, not as formal instruction. Keep the conversation light while people enter.
  • If a participant has trouble with the eWorkbook, solve only the access problem now. Save feature questions for the formal walkthrough.

Debrief and monitor

Watch for

  • If someone cannot open the link, ask them to work from a partner’s shared screen until the first break.
  • Keep this moving so the course still begins at 9:00 a.m.
Say: “As you join, please open the eWorkbook link in chat. We’ll use one workspace all day, so keep that tab open.”

Slide 4 · Poll

Where are you starting from today?

Course activity

3 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Give the room a low-risk first interaction, and give yourself a read on how much practice time the group will need.

Run it

  • Define “these situations” before launching the poll. You mean moments such as unexpected feedback, a defensive colleague, a missed handoff, or carrying a decision you did not choose.
  • Treat every response as a valid starting point. The poll is a baseline, not a score or a public confidence check.
  • Do not ask people to explain their selection. The low-risk start matters more than discussion here.

Launch the poll as you finish reading the four options. Leave it open 60 seconds. Close it and share the results to the room.

Debrief and monitor

Read the results aloud, including the numbers, so participants on audio only are included. Take no comments here.

Listen for

Common responses may cluster on options 2 and 3. Name that out loud: knowing afterward is the most common starting point, and closing that gap is what today is for.

Watch for

A room that all selects option 1. Do not challenge it. Say that today will give them harder situations than the ones they are picturing.

Say: "Answer honestly. This is not scored and I will not call on anyone about it."

Slide 11 · Chat

When did emotion change the outcome?

Course activity

6 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Surface the room’s own evidence that this matters, so you never have to argue the case from research.

Run it

  • Give participants quiet thinking time before asking them to post. A fast prompt will produce vague answers.
  • As you read responses, group them by what changed next, such as escalation, shutdown, avoidance, clearer problem solving, or recovery.
  • Do not diagnose the people in the examples. Keep the discussion on observable reactions and consequences.

Individually, in chat, 3 minutes to think and post. The instructor reads and groups responses for the remaining 3 minutes.

Debrief and monitor

  • Name the pattern: almost nobody posts an example about intelligence or effort. They post examples about reactions.
  • Read four or five aloud, including the numbers where a pattern repeats, so audio-only participants are included. Group them out loud into two buckets: the ones where a reaction made it worse, and the ones where somebody staying steady made it better.

Watch for

  • A quiet chat. Post your own example first and wait. Do not fill the silence with content.
  • A participant who names a colleague or a specific incident. Thank them, then restate the no-names instruction to the room rather than to them.
Say: "One line in chat. No names. Nothing you would not say out loud in a team meeting."

Slide 14 · Video + chat

Watch one exchange, twice

Course activity

14 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Build the observation habit the whole day depends on, using somebody else’s conversation before participants examine their own.

Run it

  • Tell participants what changes between viewings. First time, follow the exchange. Second time, watch for the moment the interaction shifts and the evidence that supports the read.
  • During debrief, keep asking “What did you see or hear?” until responses move from labels to evidence.
  • If the clip fails, use the backup link. Do not spend the activity time troubleshooting a shared stream.

Individually, in chat, after the second viewing: one word for each person. 2 minutes.

Debrief and monitor

5 minutes. Read a sample aloud. Ask what specifically told them, then push once for the observable evidence: tone, pace, word choice, what the person stopped doing.

Listen for

Listen for evidence rather than labels. "Defensive" is a label. "He started explaining before she finished the sentence" is evidence, and evidence is what they can act on.

Watch for

Participants who read intent into the clip. Redirect once: name what you saw, not why you think they did it.

Slide 17 · Individual eWorkbook

Where are you strongest today?

Private Game Board

14 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Give participants a personal baseline they will return to during action planning, so the final commitment is grounded in their own read rather than in the last thing taught.

Run it

  • Have participants open the self-assessment in the eWorkbook. They rate all four skills from 1 to 5 and name one situation where the lowest skill costs them.
  • During the debrief, discuss only the process of rating. Good prompts are “Was your lowest area what you expected?” and “Did one situation make the rating clearer?”
  • Protect privacy. If someone begins sharing more than they intended, thank them and redirect to the skill rather than the personal details.

Individual, 8 minutes, in the participant eWorkbook. Instructor stays silent for the first 5 minutes rather than narrating over it.

Debrief and monitor

Use 6 minutes. Do not collect ratings. Ask whether the lowest area was what participants expected and whether naming a specific situation changed the rating. Take two or three responses.

Listen for

Surprise about which skill scored lowest, or comments that a specific situation changed how participants rated themselves. Do not generalize from a few responses.

Watch for

Participants who rate themselves 5 across the board. Do not challenge it publicly. Say to the room that the last scenario of the day tends to move these numbers.

Say: "Rate each of the four skills 1 to 5. Then write one situation where your lowest score costs you something. Keep this open. We come back to it at the action-planning block."

Slide 18 · Poll

Which skill would help you most this quarter?

Team Board

5 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Give participants a stake in the agenda, and give yourself real data on where to spend the discretionary minutes this afternoon.

Run it

  • This poll is the first Team Board marker. It captures the room’s priority, not anyone’s private self-assessment score.
  • Share the distribution and place the class pattern on the Team Board. If one option clearly leads, spend your optional examples and debrief attention there while keeping the planned slide times intact.
  • Do not infer that the leading option is a weakness. It is the area participants say would help them most right now.
  • Launch as you finish reading the four options. Leave it open 90 seconds. Share the results to the room and read the distribution aloud.
  • Use the result as a Team Board class pattern and as a cue for where to focus optional examples and debrief time. Do not change the planned slide durations.

Debrief and monitor

Name which module covers the winning option and say you will protect its practice time. Then keep that promise, because the room will notice if you do not.

Listen for

Options 2 and 4 usually lead. If option 3 leads, plan to extend the module 4 scenario debrief and trim the module 5 discussion.

Slide 24 · Private reflection

Your three earliest signals

Private Game Board

7 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Convert the general signal list into each participant’s own, named, ordered set, which is what makes it usable next week.

Run it

  • The task is stated in full on the slide and repeated in chat, so it does not depend on hearing the instruction or seeing a diagram.
  • Keep the reflection private from start to finish. Participants are identifying their own early-warning pattern, not preparing a story to share.
  • At the halfway point, remind the room to write signals in order. If they are writing the full incident, bring them back to what they noticed first.
  • When the reflection ends, ask only whether the earliest signal was physical, attentional, or something else. Do not ask what happened in the original conversation.

Individual work in the participant eWorkbook, 4 minutes. Stay off audio so participants have quiet thinking time.

Debrief and monitor

Use 3 minutes. Ask only whether the earliest signal was physical, attentional, or something else. Do not ask participants to share the original incident.

Listen for

The majority will be physical. Name that: the body is the earlier and more reliable signal, so that is the one worth training.

Watch for

  • Participants who write a story rather than signals. Restate the task to the room at the 2-minute mark: three things you noticed, not what happened.
  • Anyone who looks distressed on camera. Do not single them out. Remind the room the exercise is private and they can pick a milder example.
Say: "Nothing in chat. Nothing shared. Write for yourself: the first three things you noticed, in order, and circle the earliest one."

Slide 27 · Private + low-risk chat share

Scenario: the feedback you did not see coming

Private Game Board + Team Board

10 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Practice all three self-awareness moves on one situation, in sequence, before any response is discussed.

Run it

  • Read the scenario aloud once. Post the three questions in chat so participants are not working from the slide alone.
  • Run the activity in two layers. First, participants complete NOTICE, NAME, and TRIGGER privately in the eWorkbook. Second, they share only one low-risk NOTICE signal for the class debrief.
  • Keep the debrief focused on noticing. If someone jumps to what they would say, hold the response for the next module.

Private eWorkbook work, 4 minutes. Then ask for one low-risk NOTICE signal in chat, 2 minutes. Use the remaining time for debrief.

Debrief and monitor

Use 4 minutes. Group the shared NOTICE signals into broad categories and connect those categories to the self-awareness marker on the Team Board.

Listen for

  • Question 1: physical signals dominate, and the two colleagues on the call almost always appear in the answer.
  • Question 2: expect embarrassed, defensive, or frustrated. Point out that the presence of an audience usually shifts the word toward embarrassed.
  • Question 3: expect being corrected in front of other people. Name it as the most commonly reported workplace trigger in the room.

Watch for

Participants who jump to what they would say. Hold them: "Not yet. Module 3 is the response. This module is the noticing."

Say: Complete all three in your eWorkbook. When I ask for the share, post only one NOTICE signal in chat. Keep the emotion word and trigger private.

Slide 31 · Breakout

Rewrite the reaction

Private Game Board + Team Board

18 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Move self-management from recognition to production. Participants write the actual words, which is the only version of this skill that transfers.

Run it

  • Before launching rooms, confirm that every room has a reaction prompt and knows it must return with one rewritten first sentence.
  • The purpose is not to write a perfect conversation. The first sentence is enough to show whether the person created space before reacting.

Give each room a different reaction drawn from the four running situations, so the debrief covers more ground. Reactions: explaining over the top of feedback, going silent for the rest of the meeting, replying to the whole team on an email thread, and agreeing in the room then complaining afterward.

Debrief and monitor

6 minutes in the main room. Take one sentence per room, in order. Write each sentence on the shared whiteboard or paste it in chat so the room can compare wording.

Listen for

Strong rewrites usually do one of three things: ask a question, name the pause, or state one fact without interpretation. Name whichever pattern the room produced.

Watch for

  • A room that produces a paragraph. Take only the first sentence and say why: the first sentence is what determines the next ten minutes.
  • A rewrite that is passive-aggressive rather than direct. Read it neutrally and ask the room how the other person would hear it.
  • A silent room. Drop in at the 5-minute mark, ask who is reporting back, and leave.
Say: "Pick someone to read the reaction aloud, and someone to report back. You need one sentence at the end, not a discussion summary."

Slide 38 · Pairs

Scenario: the colleague who goes defensive

Private Game Board + Team Board

14 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Practice reading a reaction that appears disproportionate, and produce a next sentence that does not escalate it.

Run it

  • Read the scenario aloud once, including the quoted line, in a neutral tone. Post the three questions in chat.
  • Before the breakout, remind pairs that the quoted response may be about competence or standing, but they must treat that as a hypothesis to check, not a fact.
  • Ask how each next sentence would land before discussing whether the wording is “right.” The point is to reduce escalation and gather better information.

Pairs, 7 minutes. Use the platform’s automatic pairing. Broadcast a 2-minute warning. Each pair returns with one next sentence.

Debrief and monitor

6 minutes in the main room. Take four or five sentences. Ask the room, not the author, how each one would land.

Listen for

  • Question 1: they heard a challenge to their competence, not a request for data.
  • Question 2: their expertise and their standing, not the number.
  • Question 3: the strong answers separate the request from the person, for example naming why you need the data and what you are using it for. Weak answers either apologize for asking or restate the request more firmly.

Watch for

  • Pairs who conclude the colleague is simply difficult. Push back once: that conclusion is available at the end, not at the start, and it removes every option you have.
  • A next sentence that begins by defending the question. Read it back neutrally and ask what the colleague is likely to do next.
Say: "In your pair, answer all three. You need one next sentence at the end, in the words you would actually use."

Slide 40 · Chat

The assumption you almost acted on

Private Game Board + Team Board

5 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Make the cost of a reading error personal and specific, using the room’s own material rather than a research claim.

Run it

Keep the two-line format tight. Participants post the first interpretation and the information that later corrected it.

Individual, in chat, 3 minutes to post. Instructor reads and groups responses for the remaining 2 minutes.

Debrief and monitor

Read four or five aloud, including the pattern where it repeats, so audio-only participants are included. Name the recurring shape out loud.

Listen for

The common pattern is assuming intent where the real cause was workload, missing information, or something happening outside work. Name it: people attribute behavior to character and circumstances to themselves.

Watch for

This slide is the first to compress if you are behind. Take three responses instead of five and move.

Say: "Two lines. What you assumed, and what it actually was. No names."

Slide 45 · Pairs

Scenario: your slip cost another team

Private Game Board + Team Board

14 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Practice the four-step structure from the harder side, where the participant is at fault and the temptation to explain is strongest.

Run it

  • Read the scenario aloud once. Post the four steps and the task in chat. Say explicitly that participants are the one who slipped.
  • Make the role clear before rooms open: the participant missed the handoff. The challenge is to lead with accountability rather than explanation.
  • If the room produces mixed openings, use the contrast. Ask what the other team is likely to hear first in each version.

Pairs, 7 minutes. Automatic pairing. Broadcast a 2-minute warning. Each pair returns with their opening two sentences.

Debrief and monitor

6 minutes. Take four or five openings. After each, ask the room one question: does that lead with the fact, or with the reason?

Listen for

Strong openings name the fact and the impact in the first sentence and get to what happens next quickly. Weak openings lead with the explanation, which reads as defense even when the reason is legitimate.

Watch for

  • Openings that front-load the reason. This is the single most common pattern, and it is worth naming as a pattern rather than as an individual error.
  • Over-apologising. Three apologies in ninety seconds transfers the emotional work to the other team.
  • A pair who wants to negotiate the deadline first. Note it and park it: the relationship move comes before the logistics.
Say: "Plan the first ninety seconds. You need two opening sentences in the words you would use. One person will read them out."

Slide 52 · Breakout

Scenario: carrying a change you did not choose

Private Game Board

20 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Integrate all four skills on a situation with no clean answer, which is the closest this course gets to real conditions.

Run it

  • Read the scenario aloud once. Post the scenario and the three deliverables in chat before launching rooms. Say explicitly that participants do not agree with the decision, because that constraint is what makes the scenario hard.
  • The three breakout deliverables remain the only required output: opening sentence, question, and one thing they will not say.
  • Do not add a separate game activity. The board is a reference surface for the capstone, not another task.
  • Rooms of four. Four to five rooms for a room of 16 to 20.
  • Duration 14 minutes. Set the timer and enable the return countdown.
  • Broadcast at 7 minutes and again at 3 minutes remaining.
  • Each room returns with three things: the opening sentence, the question they ask the team, and the one thing they decided not to say.
  • Ask each room to nominate a reporter in the first minute.

Debrief and monitor

  • Handled on the next slide. Do not start the debrief here, or you will lose the timing.
  • Drop into each room once, briefly. Ask only two questions: who is reporting, and what is your opening sentence. Then leave. Do not teach inside the rooms.

Watch for

  • Rooms that spend the whole time debating whether the decision was right. Drop in and redirect: you are not relitigating it, you are delivering it.
  • Rooms that write a full script. Take only the three deliverables.
  • A room that decides to tell the team they disagree. Do not correct it in the room. It is the most productive thing that can happen in the debrief.
Say: "Three deliverables, in the words you would actually use. Do not write a script for the whole meeting. The first three minutes decide the rest."

Slide 53 · Main-room debrief

Team Board: what changed in us, and around us

Team Board

10 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Debrief the breakout by mapping the room’s own output back onto the four skills, so the framework is proven rather than asserted.

Run it

  • Build the debrief in two passes. First, capture the three deliverables from every room. Second, step back and connect the patterns to SELF and TEAM.
  • For SELF, point to changes in the person’s move: noticing earlier, pausing, asking, checking a read, leading with a fact, or choosing what not to say.
  • For TEAM, point to what those choices make possible: people keep talking, disagreement stays workable, the decision stays clear, and the conversation produces information instead of shutdown.

Debrief and monitor

  • Take all three deliverables from each room in turn, in order. Keep each room to under 90 seconds.
  • Paste each opening sentence in chat or capture it on the whiteboard so the room can compare wording.
  • After all rooms report, name the pattern across them rather than ranking them.
  • If a room decided to tell the team they disagree, put it to the whole room: what does that buy the team, and what does it cost them? There's no single right answer, and saying so is more honest than ruling it out. Name the trade-off: it buys credibility in the moment and costs the team a clear place to direct their energy.

Listen for

  • Opening sentences: strong ones state the decision plainly and early. Weak ones bury it after context, which the team reads as evasion.
  • Questions: strong ones ask what the team needs to know or what concerns them first. Weak ones ask whether everyone is okay, which invites nothing.
  • What they would not say: expect "I do not agree with this either." Handle it carefully and openly, see below.

Watch for

Do not rank the rooms. The comparison is between approaches, not between groups.

Slide 55 · Individual + chat

Decision point: you have one move left

Private Game Board + Team Board

9 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Force a real choice with a defensible answer, so the module ends on judgment rather than on a framework.

Run it

  • Read the line aloud, in the voice the colleague would use. Post the four options in chat.
  • Treat every option as a trade-off. Ask what information each move gives, what it postpones, and what it may close down.
  • Do not announce a single correct answer. Use the debrief to compare how the four moves may land in this context.

Individual. Select in chat by number, 1 minute. Then one sentence of justification in chat, 3 minutes.

Debrief and monitor

5 minutes. Read the distribution aloud, then take one defense for each option that got votes. Ask the room which option the colleague would find most useful, which is a different question from which is most comfortable.

Listen for

There's no single right answer and you should say so. Option 2 is usually strongest because the question is not really a request for information, it is a request to be heard, and option 2 is the only one that finds out what is actually wrong. Option 3 is right in content and often wrong in timing. Option 1 is honest but closes the conversation. Option 4 is defensible only if you actually hold the conversation.

Watch for

  • Participants who pick option 3 because it is positive. Ask how it lands on somebody who has just been told to stop.
  • A room that unanimously picks one option. Argue the strongest alternative yourself so the trade-off is visible.

Slide 58 · Individual eWorkbook

One behavior, one situation, one date

Private Game Board

12 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Convert the day into one specific, dated commitment participants can act on after the session.

Run it

  • Keep the commitment small enough to observe. “Ask one question before I explain in Monday’s review” is stronger than “be more self-aware.”
  • Require a specific situation and a date within the next two weeks. If they cannot name both, the behavior is still too broad.

Individual, 8 minutes, in the participant eWorkbook. Instructor stays off audio for the first 5 minutes.

Debrief and monitor

4 minutes. Do not ask what anyone wrote yet. Ask instead: "Did anyone have to make their behavior smaller to name a situation for it?" Take two answers.

Listen for

Most participants start too broad, for example "be more self-aware," and have to narrow it to something like "ask one question before I answer in Monday’s review." Name that narrowing as the work.

Watch for

  • Participants who pick a behavior that depends on somebody else changing. Redirect: it has to be something they can do alone.
  • Participants who choose the highest-stakes conversation they have been avoiding. Suggest a lower-stakes rehearsal first, so the first attempt is survivable.
Say: "One behavior, not four. A named situation, not a general intention. A date inside the next two weeks. If you cannot name the situation, the behavior is too big."

Slide 59 · Chat

Commit: post your one behavior

Team Board

5 minutes
Open Participant eWorkbook
Purpose: Make the commitment public, which is the difference between an intention and a plan.

Run it

Export or save the chat transcript if the client has asked for a record of commitments. Confirm that expectation before the session rather than after.

Individual, in chat, 3 minutes. Then 2 minutes of reading.

Debrief and monitor

Read four or five aloud, including the date, so audio-only participants are included. Name the most specific one as the model, and say why: it is specific enough that they will know on Friday whether they did it.

Watch for

  • A participant who posts a general aspiration. Do not correct it publicly. Read a specific one immediately after it.
  • A quiet chat. Post your own commitment first and wait.
Say: "One line. The behavior and when. Then read three others before you close the window."
